motion: Does analytic idealism adequately explain consciousness?

bridges.burden: Show that analytic idealism adequately explains consciousness.
bridges.successCriterion: Give a coherent, comparatively economical account of experience, nature, and their apparent separation.

bridges.burden: Explain why mind is the sole ontic category and matter is appearance.
bridges.successCriterion: Show that this avoids the hard problem without losing an objective world.

bridges.burden: Explain apparently private minds within one field of subjectivity.
bridges.successCriterion: Provide a coherent dissociation account tied to observed boundaries and neural correlates.

bridges.burden: Explain why experience presents a physical world unlike reality in itself.
bridges.successCriterion: Give a reasoned account of perceptual representation and regularity.

bridges.burden: Motivate idealism against materialism and particle-based panpsychism.
bridges.successCriterion: Identify specific explanatory or ontological costs avoided by idealism.

bridges.burden: Test whether analytic idealism actually adds an adequate explanation of consciousness.
bridges.successCriterion: Identify unresolved transitions, mechanisms, or explanatory gaps without needing a complete rival metaphysics.

bridges.burden: Clarify illusionism as a method for dissolving mistaken consciousness concepts.
bridges.successCriterion: Show how targeting introspective and metacognitive errors advances inquiry without denying experience.

bridges.burden: Test what explanatory value idealism adds beyond relabeling nature mental.
bridges.successCriterion: Press for distinct explanations of regularity, representation, and causal correlations.

bridges.burden: Test whether dissociative boundaries scale from persons to nature.
bridges.successCriterion: Obtain a clear non-circular account of boundary location and mechanism.

bridges.burden: Apply empirical openness and evidential discipline to claims about mind.
bridges.successCriterion: State revising evidence and distinguish anecdotes from controlled support.

sections.title: What illusionism claims
sections.weightRationale: The opening dispute fixes whether experience is denied, which problem is targeted, and how much theory Blackmore undertakes to supply.

sections.title: Idealism and rival ontologies
sections.weightRationale: This exchange sets out the one-field ontology and tests panpsychism and the status of scientific fields.

sections.title: Regularity, perception, and mental causation
sections.weightRationale: These exchanges directly test what idealism adds and how it explains an orderly physical-looking world.

sections.title: Dissociation and private minds
sections.weightRationale: Dissociation is the proposed mechanism connecting a universal mind, individual subjects, bodies, and neural correlates.

sections.title: Experience, metacognition, and self
sections.weightRationale: The speakers distinguish bare experience from reflective self-models and locate a substantial area of agreement.

sections.title: Revisability, telepathy, and materialism
sections.weightRationale: The closing exchange reveals each side's evidential posture and connects porous dissociation to possible observations.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the wrong problem
understand how we got so deluded
moves.claimSummary: Illusionism says ordinary assumptions about consciousness are mistaken and replaces the hard problem with the meta-problem of explaining those assumptions.
moves.reasonSummary: The hard problem presupposes a dualistic arising relation, whereas examining how the misleading conception formed avoids that presupposition.

inferenceSummary.premise: The usual hard problem frames experience as arising from brain activity.
inferenceSummary.inference: That framing imports the very dualism that creates the puzzle.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Inquiry should explain the illusion-producing conception instead.

burdenContact.rationale: Defines Blackmore's actual methodological claim and its intended payoff.

moves.importanceRationale: This is the foundational statement of her position.
moves.attributionRationale: The host explicitly invites Blackmore's definition and the uninterrupted answer follows.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The captions form a clear continuous explanation.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the seeming is already a phenomenal state
you fall into infinite regress
moves.claimSummary: A specific illusionism is either harmlessly compatible with experience or incoherently denies the phenomenal state required for an illusion.
moves.reasonSummary: If seeming remains experiential the hard problem remains; if experience is an edited neuronal digest, successive digests generate a regress.

inferenceSummary.premise: An experienced illusion is itself phenomenal, while a neuronal digest is itself neuronal.
inferenceSummary.inference: Neither route eliminates the explanatory target without restating it.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Specific eliminative illusionism is incoherent and broad illusionism does no hard-problem work.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges a rival treatment of experience while preserving Kastrup's own acceptance of self-illusion.

moves.importanceRationale: It is his principal opening objection and frames the ensuing dispute.

responseComponents.description: Argues that seeming already instantiates the experience the approach seeks to explain away.

moves.attributionRationale: The host hands the floor to Kastrup and the turn is continuous.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The regress is explicitly and sequentially stated.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: something that is not what it seems to be
it's not trying to solve the hard problem
moves.claimSummary: Her illusionism does not deny experience or offer a competing consciousness theory; it is a modest approach for exposing mistaken assumptions.
moves.reasonSummary: Calling experience other than it seems redirects inquiry toward self, free-will, and consciousness illusions without claiming a full metaphysics.

inferenceSummary.premise: Illusionism is an approach, not a theory competing with IIT or global workspace.
inferenceSummary.inference: It need not solve the hard problem on the hard problem's own terms.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Its usefulness lies in diagnosing why that framing arose.

burdenContact.rationale: Limits her burden and explicitly preserves subjective states.

moves.importanceRationale: This is the burden-limiting clarification essential to assess her fairly.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the imposed eliminative definition and narrows her claim to a methodological approach.

moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore begins with explicit disagreement and speaks continuously.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The limitation and preservation of subjective states are unambiguous.
moves.spanLengthRationale: The remaining passage supplies four inseparable qualifications to this reply: experience is present, illusionism is a methodological approach, it rejects the hard problem’s framing, and its modest utility concerns several introspective illusions; cutting at the first definition would remove the answer to the specific objection.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I don't have an answer
No, I'm not a materialist
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore offers no complete rival metaphysics, but argues that illusionism exposes category mistakes while rejecting materialist production of experience.
moves.reasonSummary: The conscious/unconscious-process distinction makes little sense, and materialism recreates the hard problem by saying experience arises from brain processes.

inferenceSummary.premise: She does not know the final ontology and does not deny experience.
inferenceSummary.inference: A diagnostic approach can still reject confused distinctions and materialist emergence.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Her critique is legitimate without a completed alternative metaphysics.

burdenContact.rationale: Establishes her actual critical burden and explicitly nonmaterialist position.

moves.importanceRationale: It prevents a false materialist attribution and states the scope of her opposition.

responseComponents.description: Concedes she lacks a final answer but denies that this defeats the diagnostic critique.

moves.attributionRationale: The extended answer and direct response to the materialism question are clearly Blackmore's.
moves.materialWordingRationale: Her disclaimers and anti-materialist statement are explicit.
moves.spanLengthRationale: The same reply explicitly declines a completed rival theory, illustrates the conscious/unconscious-process category objection, and answers the moderator’s materialism clarification. All three establish the selected burden limitation. The moderator’s question is context only and is not attributed to Blackmore.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I didn't mean to ask you to give me a metaphysical theory
either useful or it is coherent
moves.claimSummary: Kastrup says he requested a definite hypothesis, not a complete metaphysics, and argues mainstream phenomenal-state denial merely postpones its core problem.
moves.reasonSummary: Frankish and Graziano are cited as denying phenomenal properties or consciousness, yet representation of phenomenal states by nonphenomenal states remains unexplained.

inferenceSummary.premise: Agreement or criticism requires a specified claim, and eliminative accounts leave the crucial representation unexplained.
inferenceSummary.inference: Broad illusion-talk is trivial while narrow denial is unstable.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Illusionism fails to be both informative and coherent.

burdenContact.rationale: Refines his objection without imposing a complete-metaphysics burden on Blackmore.

moves.importanceRationale: It is the fullest defense of his specificity dilemma.

responseComponents.description: Accepts that no complete metaphysics was requested but insists on a definite hypothesis.
Argues that broad diagnosis says too little to distinguish the view.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup explicitly clarifies his earlier request in a continuous turn.
moves.materialWordingRationale: Examples and conclusion are clearly captured.
moves.spanLengthRationale: This reply first distinguishes a definite hypothesis from a complete metaphysics, then answers Blackmore’s requests and corrections concerning Frankish and Graziano, and finally states the coherence/usefulness conclusion. The interleaved clarifying objections are context, not claims attributed to Kastrup; the complete inferential response cannot be preserved by cutting to one example.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I dissociate from his idea
the best theory we've got at the moment
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore distinguishes her weaker illusionism from Frankish and explores attention-schema and first-person practices as promising but incomplete tools.
moves.reasonSummary: Attention schemas model allocated processing without attaching qualia to objects, while meditation and altered states provide complementary evidence about experience.

inferenceSummary.premise: She rejects denial of phenomenal properties and treats Graziano's schema as incomplete.
inferenceSummary.inference: Multiple scientific, philosophical, and experiential methods can probe the illusions.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Methodological illusionism can guide inquiry without asserting a finished ontology.

burdenContact.rationale: Supplies concrete research directions and repeats her limited commitment.

moves.importanceRationale: It gives substantive content to the otherwise broad method.
moves.attributionRationale: The speaker continues from her explicit Frankish distinction into Graziano and practice.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The qualifications are stated directly.
moves.spanLengthRationale: Blackmore first expressly rejects phenomenal-property denial, then sets out the attention-schema alternative and its limitation, and finally explains why personal practice must complement scientific and philosophical inquiry. These are the selected method’s claim, concrete mechanism and methodological reason, rather than a broad transcript neighborhood.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: introspection is essential
you are perforce an idealist
moves.claimSummary: Kastrup agrees introspection is essential and argues that rejecting dualism while accepting phenomenal states leaves idealism as the available ontic category.
moves.reasonSummary: Objective studies remain valuable, but Blackmore's commitments exclude both dualism and eliminativism.

inferenceSummary.premise: Blackmore accepts experience and rejects dualist material production.
inferenceSummary.inference: Those commitments place reality within the mental category.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Her position is semantically idealist even if she rejects the label.

burdenContact.rationale: Uses shared commitments to motivate the idealist ontology.

moves.importanceRationale: It transitions from critique of illusionism to positive ontology.

responseComponents.description: Argues her accepted premises already constrain the ontological destination.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup answers her invitation and speaks continuously.
moves.materialWordingRationale: His conditional argument is explicit.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what about panpsychism
idealism isn't the only possibility
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore challenges the alleged exhaustiveness of idealism by raising panpsychism.
moves.reasonSummary: Panpsychist variants appear to retain experience without accepting Kastrup's idealism.

inferenceSummary.premise: Panpsychism is another experience-affirming option.
inferenceSummary.inference: The offered disjunction may not exhaust the possibilities.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Kastrup must defend idealism's claimed uniqueness.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests whether the positive case excludes live alternatives.

moves.importanceRationale: It prompts a major exposition of the ontology and physics.

responseComponents.description: Offers panpsychism as a counterexample to the claimed forced landing.

moves.attributionRationale: The short challenge is a clearly identified Blackmore turn.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The question is exact and complete.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are no particles
there is only one field of subjectivity
moves.claimSummary: Kastrup argues particle-based panpsychism conflicts with field theory and proposes one objective, nonlocalized field of subjectivity whose activity appears as nature.
moves.reasonSummary: Particles are excitations rather than self-existing units, while scientific fields are predictive models pointing to nonlocal underlying reality; one subjectivity also avoids the combination problem.

inferenceSummary.premise: Modern physics replaces bounded particles with field excitations and seeks unification.
inferenceSummary.inference: A many-particle consciousness ontology is ill-fitted, whereas a single nonlocalized mental field dovetails with the structure.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Objective idealism is a coherent economical interpretation of the modeled world.

burdenContact.rationale: Provides the positive one-field account and contrast with panpsychism.

moves.importanceRationale: This is the central constructive metaphysical case.

responseComponents.description: Rejects particle-based versions and subsumes essence-based versions under idealism.

moves.attributionRationale: The passage contains Kastrup’s sustained field-theoretic and idealist explanation, interrupted by Blackmore asking about other panpsychisms and the meaning of fields; those clarifications remain context, not Kastrup’s claims. His quoted statements and proposed ontology are clearly identified.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The field and subjectivity claims are repeatedly stated.
moves.spanLengthRationale: The long span is necessary because the physics argument, ontology, and combination-problem conclusion form one integrated reply.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: why do they behave the way they do
I don't know what you've gained
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore asks what calling the objective fields mental explains about stable laws and consistency.
moves.reasonSummary: Idealism appears to shift labels while materialist science already models the world's behavior.

inferenceSummary.premise: The same regular fields and laws remain after the ontological relabeling.
inferenceSummary.inference: A relabeling without added explanation gains little.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Idealism must explain its distinct advantage.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly tests the motion's adequacy requirement.

moves.importanceRationale: This is the debate's central added-value objection.

responseComponents.description: Asks why mental fields have the regularities the field account describes.

moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore's question follows the field exposition.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The challenge is plainly worded.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you avoid the hard problem of consciousness
the physical world is an internal dashboard
moves.claimSummary: Idealism removes the nonmental category and explains regular mental nature plus perception as a survival- and entropy-limited dashboard.
moves.reasonSummary: Mental processes can be regular; organisms cannot mirror unlimited world states, so perception compresses salient measurements into a useful physical presentation.

inferenceSummary.premise: Regularity is compatible with mind, and faithful mirroring would overload organisms.
inferenceSummary.inference: Evolution and entropy control favor a simplified perceptual interface.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: An objective mental world can lawfully yield a physical-looking dashboard without a hard ontological transition.

burdenContact.rationale: Explains regularity and why perceived matter differs from reality in itself.

moves.importanceRationale: It is the main positive account of physical appearance.

responseComponents.description: Argues regular mind is coherent and idealism avoids an extra ontic category while explaining representation.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup directly answers both parts of Blackmore's question.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The two-part answer is explicit.
moves.spanLengthRationale: The complete answer requires both regularity and the two linked reasons for dashboard perception.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: could be spoken by a materialist
what difference idealism makes
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore argues the dashboard story is equally available to materialism and therefore does not yet show idealism's added value.
moves.reasonSummary: Evolutionary attention and fitness-shaped perception can be described without calling the external world mental.

inferenceSummary.premise: The perceptual compression story is ontology-neutral.
inferenceSummary.inference: Shared explanatory machinery cannot by itself favor idealism.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Kastrup still owes an account of what idealism adds.

burdenContact.rationale: Distinguishes an empirical perception story from its idealist interpretation.

moves.importanceRationale: It identifies a possible gap between mechanism and metaphysics.

responseComponents.description: Argues the evolutionary account does not uniquely support idealism.

moves.attributionRationale: The response is a continuous Blackmore turn.
moves.materialWordingRationale: Her ontology-neutrality objection is explicit.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: It takes away an extra ontic category
Mental states of different kinds are modulating one another
moves.claimSummary: Idealism's gain is ontological economy: external and perceptual qualities are different mental states, so their interaction requires no mind-from-nonmind transition.
moves.reasonSummary: Thoughts, emotions, and fantasies already show qualitatively different mental states modulating one another coherently.

inferenceSummary.premise: Mental states of different kinds routinely causally modulate each other.
inferenceSummary.inference: External mental qualities can likewise modulate internal representations without changing ontic category.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Idealism preserves an external world while avoiding the hard problem.

burdenContact.rationale: States the core adequacy claim and comparative explanatory advantage.

moves.importanceRationale: This is the concise answer to what idealism adds.

responseComponents.description: Identifies removal of the nonmental category and resulting avoidance of an ontological bridge.

moves.attributionRationale: The reply alternates with Blackmore’s clarification requests about external mental qualities; the ontological-economy claim and the thoughts/emotions modulation analogy are Kastrup’s. The intervening questions are not attributed to him.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The core ontic claim is repeated clearly.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: obvious correlations between this stuff and what we feel
How can we account for that
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore presses idealism to account for bodily mechanisms and their robust correlations with felt emotion rather than dissolving them into a single label.
moves.reasonSummary: Neurotransmitters, hormones, neuronal firing, and bodily feelings exhibit correlations that any adequate view must explain.

inferenceSummary.premise: Mental changes track detailed bodily and neural changes.
inferenceSummary.inference: Calling both mental does not by itself account for those structured correlations.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Idealism needs a specific mind-body correlation account.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests whether ontic unification supplies explanatory structure.

moves.importanceRationale: It sharpens the general relabeling concern into an empirical demand.

responseComponents.description: Asks how the analogy maps onto concrete neural and bodily correlations.

moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore's reflective question is clearly hers.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The cited mechanisms and demand are explicit.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: all matter is a dashboard representation
observed from across a dissociative boundary
moves.claimSummary: Matter, including brains, is how mental processes appear when observed across a dissociative boundary.
moves.reasonSummary: If matter is the extrinsic dashboard image of inner mentality, neural-experiential correlations are two perspectives on one process rather than production across categories.

inferenceSummary.premise: Bodies and neurons are material appearances of dissociated mental activity.
inferenceSummary.inference: Changes in the appearance should correlate with changes in the inner experience.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Idealism accounts for neural correlations without generating consciousness from matter.

burdenContact.rationale: Introduces dissociation as the bridge between inner experience and observable biology.

moves.importanceRationale: It is the key idealist account of mind-brain correlation.

responseComponents.description: Recasts neural and experiential changes as extrinsic and intrinsic aspects of one mental process.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup directly answers the correlation question.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The dissociative-boundary formulation is explicit.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the simplest understanding of a dissociative boundary
a sort of minimal dissociative boundary
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore asks for a minimal, clear definition of a dissociative boundary and how boundaries are individuated.
moves.reasonSummary: Kastrup's account seems to invoke boundaries within organisms, between persons, and between persons and the world without yet specifying the common criterion.

inferenceSummary.premise: The explanatory work depends on identifying dissociative boundaries.
inferenceSummary.inference: Ambiguous boundary criteria weaken the proposed mechanism.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: A minimal operational account is required.

burdenContact.rationale: Targets the core individuation mechanism rather than demanding a rival theory.

moves.importanceRationale: It initiates the most detailed mechanism-focused exchange.

responseComponents.description: Requests the criterion needed for the proposed intrinsic-extrinsic relation.

moves.attributionRationale: The original inventory describes consecutive host and Blackmore clarification questions without establishing exactly who owns each boundary-request sentence. Verify the short mixed-turn passage before judgments; credit only Blackmore’s own request and reason.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The minimal-boundary request is repeated.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: given by inferential isolation
Dissociation can do that
moves.claimSummary: Conceptually dissociation is inferential isolation, and clinically it can block access so strongly that a sighted person lacks visual-cortex activity under a blind alter.
moves.reasonSummary: The reported dissociative-identity study supplies an objective correlate of radically partitioned access, while ordinary forgetting illustrates softer degrees.

inferenceSummary.premise: Dissociation can produce measurable, state-dependent informational isolation.
inferenceSummary.inference: Mental activity can divide into centers lacking access to one another.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Inferential isolation is an empirically grounded model for private perspectives.

burdenContact.rationale: Defines the mechanism and supplies its main empirical analogy.

moves.importanceRationale: This is the direct answer to the boundary request.

responseComponents.description: Defines the boundary through inferential isolation and illustrates its graded effects.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup begins with the conceptual answer and continues through the study.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The definition is clear; study details are presented as his report.
moves.spanLengthRationale: The definition and empirical case jointly constitute the complete offered answer.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how this kind of relates to idealism
find these boundaries in the world
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore accepts person-level dissociation but questions its extension to a world made entirely of mental stuff.
moves.reasonSummary: Brain-function examples do not establish where organism-world boundaries come from or what the minimal world-scale boundary is.

inferenceSummary.premise: Clinical dissociation occurs within a human system.
inferenceSummary.inference: Scaling that phenomenon to divisions of universal mentality requires an additional argument.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: The empirical analogy alone does not establish idealism's cosmic boundaries.

burdenContact.rationale: Pinpoints the extrapolation from clinical evidence to metaphysics.

moves.importanceRationale: It identifies the main scope gap in the dissociation evidence.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the local case while disputing its unargued world-scale extension.

moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore explicitly contrasts brain function with the whole-world claim.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The extrapolation challenge is precise.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: life, biology, is what dissociation at a higher level looks like
they look like the neural correlates of consciousness
moves.claimSummary: Biology is the outward appearance of nature's dissociative processes, and neural correlates are the appearance of mental processes inside those living boundaries.
moves.reasonSummary: Reported imaging distinguishes genuine dissociation from acting, showing dissociation has an identifiable extrinsic pattern; idealism generalizes that intrinsic-extrinsic relation to life.

inferenceSummary.premise: Dissociation has observable biological signatures.
inferenceSummary.inference: Under idealism, biology can mark the extrinsic boundary of a dissociated subject.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Living organisms supply the sought boundary and neural correlates display their inner mentality.

burdenContact.rationale: Provides Kastrup's explicit answer for where world-scale dissociative boundaries appear.

moves.importanceRationale: This completes the central dissociation proposal.

responseComponents.description: Identifies life and metabolism as the observable boundary of dissociated centers.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup directly supplies another study and states his generalization.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The generalization is explicitly labeled his claim.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: look straight at something and not see it
shortcuts to say
moves.claimSummary: Ordinary attention already explains seeing without looking at every item and failing to notice visible items, without supporting idealism.
moves.reasonSummary: Inattentional blindness and texture-detection shortcuts separate retinal input, processing, report, and what people later say they saw.

inferenceSummary.premise: Perceptual access and report dissociate through ordinary cognitive mechanisms.
inferenceSummary.inference: Dissociation-like effects do not uniquely support metaphysical idealism.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Such phenomena are relevant to consciousness but ontology-neutral.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests whether the cited phenomena discriminate idealism from cognitive explanations.

moves.importanceRationale: It supplies an alternative interpretation of the empirical examples.
moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore gives personal research context and two clear demonstrations.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The examples and limitation are explicit.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the difference between phenomenal states
There is never such a thing as strictly unconscious states
moves.claimSummary: Kastrup distinguishes phenomenal experience from metaconscious report and argues inattentional cases concern their dissociation, not absence of experience.
moves.reasonSummary: Visual processing may continue without report, just as breathing is experienced without attention; apparent unconsciousness may therefore be absent meta-awareness.

inferenceSummary.premise: Attention is required for explicit awareness of an experience but not necessarily for the experience itself.
inferenceSummary.inference: Failure to report does not demonstrate a nonphenomenal state.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Ordinary dissociations support separating experience from metaconsciousness.

burdenContact.rationale: Defends ubiquitous phenomenality against unconscious-state interpretations.

moves.importanceRationale: It converts the perceptual examples into a key conceptual distinction.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes preserved visual experience from absent attention and report.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup explicitly replies that the mechanisms differ.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The experience/meta-awareness distinction is carefully stated.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: all that metacognitive stuff is speculations that are untrue
it's not happening to anybody
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore locates her illusionism chiefly in false metacognitive stories of a self attending and owning experience, while remaining agnostic about the underlying processes.
moves.reasonSummary: Meditative experience can retain happening while the sense of owner, time, and space disappears, suggesting those reflective constructions are not essential to experience.

inferenceSummary.premise: Experience can persist when self-reflective interpretation falls away.
inferenceSummary.inference: The owner and narrative are constructed metacognitive additions.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Illusionism should target those additions rather than deny underlying experience.

burdenContact.rationale: Gives the most specific formulation of Blackmore's introspective illusion claim.

moves.importanceRationale: It narrows the view and reveals convergence without surrendering agnosticism.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the distinction but identifies the metacognitive self-story as the illusion.

moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore responds in the first person and describes her practice.
moves.materialWordingRationale: Her agnosticism and specific target are direct.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the history of science is the history of illusion
it becomes a useless word
moves.claimSummary: Kastrup maintains that an overly broad definition of illusionism lacks discriminating content.
moves.reasonSummary: Nearly every scientific discovery shows appearances differ from reality, so that generic fact cannot identify a distinctive consciousness thesis.

inferenceSummary.premise: Almost nothing studied by science is exactly as it seems.
inferenceSummary.inference: A label applying to nearly everything specifies little.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Illusionism needs a narrower target to be useful.

burdenContact.rationale: Preserves the specificity objection after areas of agreement emerge.

moves.importanceRationale: It is a concise restatement tied to the clarified view.

responseComponents.description: Questions whether the proposed label discriminates enough even after experiential clarification.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup explicitly states discomfort and gives his reason.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The breadth argument is compact and clear.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the whole idea that consciousness
the way people talk about consciousness
moves.claimSummary: Blackmore specifies that the illusion is people's metalevel conception of consciousness as a separable thing produced by the brain.
moves.reasonSummary: Clearing away that conceptual objectification can prevent theorists and experimenters from repeatedly presupposing brain-produced consciousness.

inferenceSummary.premise: People reify consciousness and contrast it with matter and unconscious states.
inferenceSummary.inference: Those concepts generate the misleading production problem.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Exposing introspective and theoretical reification is genuine progress.

burdenContact.rationale: Answers the specificity demand with a bounded conceptual target.

moves.importanceRationale: This is her clearest final definition of the illusion.

responseComponents.description: Restricts the claim to concepts about minds rather than all scientific appearances.

moves.attributionRationale: Blackmore begins with a direct qualification and maintains the floor.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The targeted concepts are enumerated.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I sympathize completely
All material things are representations of mental states
moves.claimSummary: Kastrup agrees the personal self and ingrained dualist categories are illusions, then uses idealism to reinterpret apparent physical-to-mental causation as mental-to-mental interaction.
moves.reasonSummary: A needle or wine is, on his view, the dashboard appearance of transpersonal mental activity crossing a dissociative boundary, so no independent physical cause is admitted.

inferenceSummary.premise: Idealism treats material objects as representations of mental processes.
inferenceSummary.inference: Apparent physical causes are appearances of mental causes.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: The causal objection presupposes the dualism that idealism rejects.

burdenContact.rationale: Shows how the ontology handles a familiar causal challenge and marks agreement on self-illusion.

moves.importanceRationale: It applies the framework to concrete causal examples.

responseComponents.description: Agrees with the diagnosis but replaces the broad label with a specific idealist reinterpretation.

moves.attributionRationale: Kastrup explicitly sympathizes and develops his example.
moves.materialWordingRationale: The causal interpretation is stated repeatedly.
